title: AI From Scratch
description: Learn artificial intelligence from first principles: Python, mathematics, data, machine learning, deep learning, vision, NLP, transformers, generative AI, RAG, agents, deployment and AI system design.
source: Original curriculum informed by the supplied AI From Scratch reference volumes

blocks.text: Start with a mental model

Artificial intelligence is the broad goal of making systems perform tasks that normally need human judgment. Machine learning is one way to do it: a program learns a pattern from examples instead of receiving every rule by hand.

lessons.title: What AI is - and is not

blocks.text: What you will learn

Distinguish AI, machine learning and deep learning.
Recognize prediction, generation and decision-making tasks.
Describe a useful AI problem in terms of inputs and outputs.
The simple picture

A rules-based program follows instructions written by a person. A learning system receives examples, adjusts internal parameters, and makes a prediction for a new example. AI is not magic or a database that knows everything; it is a system with a goal, data, assumptions, and failure modes.
Term: feature -> a measurable input, such as floor area. Label -> the answer the model should learn to predict, such as house price.
Practice
For a spam filter, write down three possible features, the label, and one way a bad dataset could mislead the model.
Interview check
Q: What is the difference between AI and ML? A: AI is the broad field of intelligent behaviour; ML is a data-driven technique within it.
From question to useful system
A dependable workflow is: define success, collect and understand data, split data, train a baseline, evaluate, improve, deploy, then monitor. The model is only one link in this chain.

Stage | Question
Problem | What decision will this help?
Data | Is it representative and permitted?
Evaluation | What failure is costly?
Monitoring | Is live data changing?
Common mistake: starting with a complex model before defining the target metric and a simple baseline.
Mini challenge
Choose a student-support use case. Define the user, one measurable outcome, a baseline, and a risk that needs a human review.
Why this matters

Models can reproduce gaps in their data, expose sensitive information, or sound confident when wrong. Responsible work means testing across relevant groups, protecting data, documenting limits, and giving people a safe escalation path.

Use only necessary data.
Test important slices, not only one average score.
Make uncertainty and limitations visible.
Keep a human decision-maker for high-impact outcomes.
Quick quiz
Why can high accuracy still be unsafe? Because accuracy can hide harmful errors in a smaller but important group or ignore the cost of different mistakes.
Math is a language for model behaviour

You do not need to memorize formulas before you can build. Learn each tool through the job it does: vectors represent examples, probability represents uncertainty, statistics summarizes evidence, and calculus tells a model how to improve.
Intuition

A scalar is one number. A vector is an ordered list, such as the features of one house. A matrix is a rectangular table, such as many houses. The dot product combines matching values and is the core operation behind a neuron.

weights = [0.5, 0.2]
features = [100, 3]
score = sum(w * x for w, x in zip(weights, features))
print(score)
Expected output: 50.6. Here the model gives more influence to the first feature because its weight is larger.
Use matrix multiplication to apply the same operation to many examples efficiently.
Practice
Change the weights and explain how the score changes. Then identify which weight represents the strongest influence.
Useful questions

Probability asks how likely an event is. Statistics estimates patterns from a sample. Mean describes a typical value; variance describes spread. Conditional probability asks about an event after learning new information, which is the idea behind Bayes' theorem.

scores = [72, 80, 88, 90]
mean = sum(scores) / len(scores)
variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in scores) / len(scores)
print(mean, variance)
Correlation means two values move together; it does not prove one causes the other.
Interview check
Q: Why use a validation set? A: It estimates performance while tuning choices, before the final unbiased test evaluation.
The hill-walking idea

A loss function says how wrong a prediction is. A derivative measures how the loss changes when one parameter moves. A gradient collects those changes. Gradient descent takes a small step in the direction that reduces loss.

x = 8.0
learning_rate = 0.1
for _ in range(10):
    gradient = 2 * x  # derivative of x squared
    x = x - learning_rate * gradient
print(round(x, 3))
Expected output approaches 0. A learning rate that is too large can overshoot; one that is too small can make training slow.
Concept check
A partial derivative changes one parameter while holding the others fixed. Neural networks need it because they have many parameters.

chapters.title: Python and Data Handling for AI

blocks.text: Build reproducible habits
Use Python to inspect, clean and transform data before modelling. A small, reproducible notebook or script is more valuable than an unexplained model.
Keep data code readable

def normalize(values):
    low, high = min(values), max(values)
    return [(value - low) / (high - low) for value in values]

print(normalize([10, 20, 30]))
Expected output: [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]. Functions make preprocessing testable and reusable.
Practice
Write a function that returns only passing scores from a list, then add a short test for an empty list.
Garbage in, confident garbage out

Check schema, missing values, duplicates, impossible values, units, labels, and data leakage. Split training, validation and test data before fitting transformations that learn from the data, such as scaling.

Training set: fit model parameters.
Validation set: choose settings.
Test set: final once-only estimate.
Leakage: information that would not exist at prediction time.
Common mistake: normalizing the whole dataset before splitting, which lets test information influence training.
Ask simple questions first
Inspect row counts, target balance, ranges, missingness, and relationships. A chart is useful when it changes a decision: for example, identifying outliers or an imbalanced label.
Mini project
Create a dataset report for a public CSV: document each column, missing-value policy, likely leakage risks, and one question the data cannot answer.
Models learn a mapping
Supervised learning maps features to known labels. Unsupervised learning searches for structure without labels. Your first target should be a trustworthy baseline, not the most fashionable algorithm.

Task | Output | Example
Regression | number | predict rent
Classification | category or probability | detect spam
Clustering | groups | segment customers
Choose the task from the real output you need, not from the tool you want to use.
Practice
Classify these: disease-risk score, product category, similar-news groups.

A baseline is a simple reference: predict the average price, choose the most common label, or use a small linear model. Generalization means performing well on new examples, not merely memorizing training data.
Overfitting: training score looks great while validation score is weak. Underfitting: both are weak.
Interview check
Q: Why is a baseline important? A: It proves whether additional complexity creates meaningful value.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = [[1], [2], [3], [4]]
y = [2, 4, 6, 8]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.predict([[5]]))
The split happens before fitting. random_state makes the example repeatable.
Exercise
Replace the data with a small real dataset and report a metric on held-out examples.
Learn from examples with answers
Start with linear and logistic regression, then compare local methods, trees and ensembles. There is no universally best model; data size, interpretability, latency and error cost all matter.
Linear regression predicts a number. Logistic regression predicts a class probability by passing a weighted score through a sigmoid curve.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
X = [[0], [1], [2], [3]]
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
print(model.predict_proba([[2]])[0])
A probability threshold is a business decision. Lowering it often increases recall and decreases precision.

KNN uses nearby labelled examples. Naive Bayes uses probability with a simplifying independence assumption and is often a useful text baseline. An SVM seeks a boundary with a large margin between classes.

Model | Strength | Limitation
KNN | intuitive local patterns | slow predictions at scale
Naive Bayes | fast sparse-text baseline | assumptions can be too simple
SVM | effective clear margins | requires careful scaling and tuning
Practice
Explain why feature scaling is especially important for distance-based KNN and margin-based SVM.

A decision tree repeatedly asks questions that reduce uncertainty. Random forests average many diverse trees to reduce variance. Gradient boosting builds small models sequentially to correct earlier errors; XGBoost is a widely used optimized boosting implementation.
Tree models can capture nonlinear relationships and need less scaling, but deep single trees often overfit.
Mini challenge
Train a simple tree and a random forest on the same split. Compare validation score, feature importance carefully, and the likely production trade-off.
Find useful structure without answers
Unsupervised learning helps explore data, compress features, and discover groups. Treat discovered groups as hypotheses to validate, not automatic truth.
K-means alternates: assign each point to its nearest center, then move each center to the mean of its assigned points. It works best for compact, roughly round groups on a meaningful scale.
Choose k with domain knowledge plus diagnostics such as the elbow curve; never pick a number just because the chart looks tidy.
Practice
Before clustering customers, decide whether age, spending and visits need scaling and which action each cluster would support.

Principal Component Analysis finds new directions that explain large amounts of variation. Eigenvectors give directions; eigenvalues indicate how much variation they capture. PCA can simplify visualization and reduce noise, but components may be hard to explain.
Concept check
PCA preserves variance, not necessarily the information that best predicts your target.

An anomaly is an unusual observation under a chosen definition. Modern systems often represent items as embeddings: numeric vectors whose distance reflects learned similarity. Similarity is useful only after you validate it on your task.
Exercise
Design a fraud-review queue. Define what counts as unusual, how reviewers give feedback, and how you avoid treating a rare but legitimate user as automatically fraudulent.
Measure the errors that matter
Good evaluation connects model errors to the decision being made. Feature engineering converts raw information into useful, available-at-prediction-time signals.

Accuracy is the fraction correct. Precision asks: when we predicted positive, how often were we right? Recall asks: of actual positives, how many did we find? F1 balances precision and recall. ROC-AUC measures ranking across thresholds.

Regression | Meaning
MAE | average absolute error
MSE/RMSE | penalizes larger errors more
R-squared | variance explained relative to a mean baseline
For an imbalanced fraud task, accuracy can be misleading: a model that predicts 'not fraud' for everything can score highly.

Useful features are valid at prediction time, stable, understandable enough to audit, and related to the target. Selection can remove redundant or noisy fields, but must happen inside validation to avoid leakage.
Common mistakes

Using future information.
Encoding an ID as if it were a meaningful number.
Fitting preprocessing on test data.
Interpreting correlation as causation.

Cross-validation rotates validation folds so your estimate is less dependent on one split. Hyperparameters are choices made before training, such as tree depth or learning rate. Keep the test set untouched until your final decision.
Interview check
Q: Why is nested validation useful? A: It separates tuning from performance estimation when many choices are compared.
From one neuron to a trainable network

A neuron computes a weighted sum, adds a bias, then applies an activation. A network stacks these transformations to learn complex patterns. Training means reducing a loss with gradient-based optimization.

The perceptron is a weighted sum followed by a threshold. Modern networks use smooth activations such as ReLU so gradients can guide learning. Forward propagation is the pass from inputs to prediction.
Expected output: 0.9. The weights and bias are learned from data, not hand-picked in a real model.
A loss compares prediction with truth. Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule to find how every parameter contributed to loss. Optimizers such as SGD and Adam turn gradients into updates.
Batch size, learning rate, initialization and normalization all influence training stability.
Practice
Draw the flow: input -> layers -> prediction -> loss -> gradients -> updated weights.

import torch
from torch import nn

x = torch.tensor([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
y = torch.tensor([[2.0], [4.0], [6.0]])
model = nn.Linear(1, 1)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
for _ in range(100):
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
print(model(torch.tensor([[4.0]])).item())
The important order is: compute loss, clear old gradients, backpropagate, then update. Output should approach 8.

Dropout temporarily hides some units during training. Weight decay discourages overly large weights. Early stopping stops when validation performance no longer improves. Transfer learning starts from a model trained on a related large dataset, then adapts it to your task.
Interview check
Q: Why can dropout improve validation performance while making training harder? A: It prevents co-adaptation and acts as regularization.
Teach systems to work with images
Images are arrays of pixel values. A color image usually has red, green and blue channels. Vision systems must handle lighting, viewpoint, backgrounds and data quality.

A convolutional filter scans a small region and detects a local pattern, such as an edge. Stacking convolutional layers builds richer features. Pooling or striding reduces spatial size. CNNs use shared filters, which is why they are efficient for images.
Practice
Explain why an image classifier trained only on studio photos may fail on phone photos outdoors.

Task | Output
Classification | one label per image
Object detection | boxes and labels
Segmentation | label for each pixel
Select the task from the user need. A safety inspection might require detection; a medical-region analysis may require segmentation and specialist review.
Accuracy alone is not enough for detection or segmentation; use task-appropriate localization metrics and inspect qualitative failures.

Augmentation creates realistic variations during training. Image embeddings enable similarity search. Vision Transformers split an image into patches and apply attention. Grad-CAM can highlight regions influencing a CNN prediction, but it is an aid for inspection, not proof of correctness.
Project
Build an image classifier with transfer learning, an error gallery, and a short model card describing its data, limits and intended use.
Language needs representation
NLP converts text into representations a model can use while preserving enough meaning for the task. Meaning depends on context, language, domain and the people represented in the data.

Tokenization splits text into units. Stopword removal, stemming and lemmatization can help traditional pipelines, but should be chosen for the task and language. Bag of Words counts tokens; TF-IDF downweights terms common across many documents.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
texts = ['good course', 'good practical course']
features = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(texts)
print(features.shape)
Expected output is a document-by-vocabulary matrix shape.

Embeddings map words, sentences or documents to vectors. Similar meanings can end up closer in vector space, allowing semantic search beyond exact keyword matching. Word2Vec learns these patterns from context; modern transformer embeddings are contextual.
Embedding similarity is a ranking signal, not a factual guarantee.

lessons.title: Text classification, NER and sequence models

blocks.text: Text classification labels a document, for example sentiment. Named Entity Recognition identifies spans such as people or organizations. RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs process sequences step by step; attention and transformers address their difficulty with distant context.
Mini project
Create a support-ticket router. Evaluate by class, review misrouted tickets, and define a confidence threshold that sends uncertain cases to a human.
Attention lets a token look at relevant context
Transformers use attention instead of processing every token strictly one at a time. This makes training highly parallel and gives the model flexible access to context.

Each token creates a Query, Key and Value. A Query asks what is relevant; Keys describe what each token offers; Values carry information to combine. Dot products score relevance, softmax turns scores into weights, then weighted Values form a contextual representation.
Multi-head attention repeats this with several learned perspectives, allowing different relationships to be captured.
Visual in words
Token -> Q/K/V projections -> relevance scores -> softmax weights -> weighted values -> contextual token vector.

Attention alone does not know token order, so position information is added. A transformer block combines attention, a feed-forward network, residual connections and normalization. Decoder-only models use a causal mask so a token cannot view future tokens during next-token prediction.
Interview check
Q: Why do residual connections help? A: They give information and gradients a direct path through deep stacks.

Encoder models such as BERT build bidirectional representations for understanding tasks. Decoder models such as GPT generate tokens autoregressively. Encoder-decoder architectures are useful for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation.
Practice
Choose an architecture for document classification, summarization, and translation; explain your choice in one sentence each.
Generate, do not merely classify

Generative models learn a distribution that can produce new text, images, audio or structured content. Large language models predict the next token repeatedly, then are adapted to be useful in conversation and tools.

A discriminative model separates or predicts labels. A generative model can create new samples. GANs train a generator and discriminator in competition; diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual noising process. Foundation models can be adapted to many tasks.
Concept check
A text classifier can decide whether a review is positive. A language model can write a review-like continuation. They may share components but solve different objectives.

Tokenization turns text into model units. Pretraining learns next-token prediction on broad data. Fine-tuning and instruction tuning adapt behaviour. Preference training methods such as RLHF use human feedback concepts to improve helpfulness, but no alignment method removes the need for evaluation and safeguards.
Context window means the amount of token context available for one request; it is not a durable memory of every previous conversation.

At inference, a model produces token probabilities. Temperature changes randomness; top-k limits candidates; top-p samples from the smallest likely set whose total probability reaches p. Prompt engineering means clearly specifying role, task, constraints, examples, output format and evaluation criteria.
Structured output
For software, ask for a validated schema rather than prose when you need reliable downstream processing. Validate output server-side even when the model follows the format.
Exercise
Write a prompt that extracts title, date and action items as JSON, including instructions for missing information.
Give the model grounded context
RAG retrieves relevant information at request time and supplies it to an LLM. It is useful when knowledge changes, needs citations, or must come from trusted private documents.

Documents -> extraction -> chunking -> embeddings -> vector index -> similarity search -> selected context -> LLM answer. Each arrow can fail, so evaluate the pipeline as a system, not only the final answer.
Chunking controls the trade-off between focused retrieval and enough surrounding context. Preserve document metadata such as source and section.
Why not just put everything in the prompt?
Large prompts cost more, can exceed context limits, and make it harder for the model to focus on the relevant evidence.

An embedding model represents queries and chunks as vectors. Cosine similarity or another distance ranks candidates. A reranker can make a more precise second pass. Hybrid retrieval combines semantic and keyword signals when exact terms matter.
Practice
For an employee handbook assistant, list metadata filters that prevent a user from retrieving another department's private documents.

Retrieval failure: correct evidence was never found.
Context failure: evidence was found but badly selected or truncated.
Generation failure: answer ignores evidence or invents detail.
Permission failure: retrieval exposes information the user should not see.
Evaluate retrieval recall, citation correctness, answer faithfulness, latency and safety. Log anonymized traces, inspect failures, and provide a fallback when evidence is insufficient.
Project
Build a document assistant that cites chunks, refuses unsupported answers, and includes a small evaluation set with expected sources.
An agent is an orchestrated loop

An AI agent observes context, selects a next action, may call a tool, records the result, and decides whether to continue. A chatbot can be an agent, but an agent differs by reliably acting through bounded tools and workflows.

lessons.title: Tools, state and the agent loop

blocks.text: A minimal loop is: receive goal -> inspect allowed state -> choose tool -> validate tool arguments -> execute -> observe result -> decide next step or stop. Tools should have narrow schemas and predictable errors.

while not done:
    action = choose_next_action(state, allowed_tools)
    result = run_validated_tool(action)
    state = update_state(state, result)
Never give an agent unrestricted access just because it can reason about a task. Limit permissions, cost and loop count.

Planning can split a goal into steps; memory can store user-approved facts or task state. Both can be wrong. Guardrails validate inputs and outputs, enforce authorization, constrain sensitive actions, and route uncertain cases to humans.
Evaluation

Test agents with realistic tasks, tool errors, adversarial instructions, cost limits and explicit success criteria. Measure whether the final action was correct, not merely whether the explanation sounded plausible.

Start with one workflow: search approved sources, summarize with citations, and ask a human before publishing. Add tools only when evaluation shows they help. Avoid multi-agent complexity until one agent is reliable.
Interview check
Q: How do you prevent destructive agent actions? A: scoped tools, allowlists, confirmation gates, idempotent operations, audit logs and evaluation.
A model becomes a product through engineering
Serving a model safely needs more than saving weights. You need versioned artifacts, an API contract, reproducible environments, observability, security and a rollback plan.

Model serialization stores trained artifacts. A FastAPI service can validate a request, transform input exactly as training did, call the model, and return a versioned response. Keep secrets in environment variables, never source code.
Start with a health endpoint and a clear request/response schema before connecting a model.

Version code, data references, model artifacts and configurations together. Experiment tracking records parameters, metrics and artifacts so results are comparable. CI runs checks automatically; CD promotes a tested version through environments.
Reproducibility is the ability to explain and recreate a result, not simply to rerun a notebook once.

Monitor latency, error rate, throughput, cost, input drift, output quality and safety events. CPU inference can be appropriate for small or low-volume models; GPUs accelerate many neural workloads. Scale only after measuring the bottleneck.
Production checklist

Authentication and authorization.
Rate limits and input validation.
Structured logs and request tracing.
Canary release or rollback path.
Human escalation for consequential errors.
Design around the decision, not the model
A robust AI system makes requirements, data flow, storage, model boundaries, APIs, caching, monitoring and failure handling explicit before implementation.

Begin with users, decisions, latency, quality, privacy, cost and unacceptable failures. Then sketch the flow: client -> API -> authorization -> retrieval or model -> validation -> response -> telemetry. Every component should earn its complexity.
Design exercise
Design a recommendation system. Define the event data, offline training job, online feature lookup, ranking API, feedback loop and metrics beyond click-through rate.

Separate deterministic application logic from probabilistic model output. Validate schema, retrieve only authorized evidence, cache safe repeated work, set time and spend budgets, and show citations or uncertainty where relevant.
Do not use an LLM to enforce permissions. Authorization belongs in deterministic application code before retrieval or tool execution.

Clarify user and success metric.
Estimate scale and constraints.
Draw the happy-path data flow.
Discuss storage, model choice and APIs.
Address reliability, safety, observability and cost.
Name trade-offs and a phased launch plan.
Interview check
Q: How do you evaluate an AI system? A: with component metrics, end-to-end task success, slice-based quality, reliability, latency, cost and human feedback.
Turn learning into evidence
Projects demonstrate your ability to define a problem, make choices, evaluate results and communicate limitations. Build fewer projects with clearer evidence rather than many cloned notebooks.

Level | Project | Evidence
Beginner | spam classifier or house-price predictor | clean split and metric
Intermediate | image classifier or sentiment system | error analysis and model card
Advanced | semantic search or RAG assistant | retrieval evaluation and citations
Capstone | full AI application | frontend, API, auth, database, monitoring
Choose a domain you understand. Start with a baseline, write down assumptions, and keep a short decision log.

Build a production-style document assistant: a web interface sends authenticated requests to an API; documents are extracted, chunked and embedded; access-controlled retrieval selects evidence; the LLM returns a cited answer; logs and evaluation traces reveal failures.
Definition of done

A reproducible ingestion pipeline.
Permission-aware retrieval.
Cited answers and abstention when evidence is missing.
A test set with retrieval and answer checks.
Deployment notes, monitoring and cost budget.

Use a concise structure: problem, users, data, baseline, model choice, evaluation, failure analysis, deployment and next improvement. Be specific about what did not work. Honest trade-offs demonstrate engineering judgment.
Questions to rehearse

How did you prevent leakage?
Why did you select this metric?
Which failures were most important?
How would you monitor drift?
How would you reduce latency or cost?
What required human oversight?
Course completion challenge
Publish a portfolio-ready README containing architecture, setup, evaluation, screenshots, limitations and a responsible-use note.
